prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: EN · Plan comparison (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Feature" · longest unbreakable word 56px · one-line width 83px
  col 2: header "Free" · longest unbreakable word 79px · one-line width 79px
  col 3: header "Pro" · longest unbreakable word 66px · one-line width 66px
  col 4: header "Enterprise" · longest unbreakable word 75px · one-line width 229px
  col 5: header "Notes" · longest unbreakable word 73px · one-line width 419px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

These are all candidate designs you produced, rendered in a real browser:
Design r1B: widths [115, 100, 87, 170, 247] · table 720×312px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 60, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 2 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r1C: widths [110, 100, 90, 200, 219] · table 720×335px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 83, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r2A: widths [106, 100, 90, 180, 243] · table 720×312px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 60, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 2 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r2B: widths [106, 100, 90, 192, 231] · table 720×335px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 83, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r2C: widths [106, 100, 90, 175, 248] · table 720×312px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 60, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 2 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r3A: widths [105, 100, 88, 175, 251] · table 720×312px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 60, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 2 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r3B: widths [105, 100, 88, 170, 256] · table 720×312px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 60, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 2 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r3C: widths [105, 100, 88, 180, 246] · table 720×312px · row heights [36, 60, 60, 60, 36, 60] · column headers wrapped 0/5 · tallest cell 2 lines · mid-word splits 0

Decide as a designer:
- "preferred": the best design(s). Name more than one only if they are genuinely equally good.
- "acceptable": other designs a careful designer would still publish.
- "bad": designs with clear visual faults, each with the fault. If none of these is clearly bad, also return ONE deliberately bad but plausible alternative as "contrast" widths and say what is wrong with it.
- "ranges": for each column, the px range within which the preferred design stays equally good (keep other columns' proportions).
- "rationale": 2–4 concrete sentences about this table.
- "principles": observations that seem GENERAL (likely to hold for other tables) vs SPECIFIC to this case.
- "tradeoffs" and "uncertain": what reasonable designers could disagree on.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"preferred":["name"],"acceptable":["name"],"bad":[{"design":"name","why":""}],"contrast":{"widths":[int px],"why":""} or null,"ranges":[[min,max]],"rationale":"","principles":{"general":[""],"specific":[""]},"tradeoffs":"","uncertain":""}

log.raw: {"preferred":["r2C"],"acceptable":["r1B","r2A","r3A","r3B","r3C"],"bad":[{"design":"r1C","why":"Notes is squeezed to 219px, so the SSO note breaks into three lines and orphans “provider.”; the resulting 83px row breaks the otherwise 60px row rhythm and makes the table 335px tall."},{"design":"r2B","why":"Notes at 231px causes the same three-line SSO note with an orphaned “provider.” and an isolated 83px row; the extra Enterprise width is not worth the uneven vertical rhythm."}],"contrast":null,"ranges":[[104,112],[100,106],[87,94],[170,180],[246,251]],"rationale":"r2C is the best balance: Free stays at its 100px minimum for “Community,” Pro has a little slack at 90px for “Unlimited,” and Feature is just above the 104px needed to keep “SSO / SAML” on one line. Its 248px Notes column keeps the SSO note to two lines and avoids the orphaned “provider.” that makes r1C/r2B taller, while 175px Enterprise wraps the support value into two acceptable lines. The result is a 312px table with uniform 60px rows, no wrapped headers, and no mid-word splits.","principles":{"general":["Column widths should be driven by the longest unbreakable token and the desired line break, not by equal widths.","A single three-line row among two-line rows creates a visible rhythm break; allocate enough width to the secondary notes column to prevent avoidable orphans.","Do not starve a secondary column to overfeed a primary column once the primary column’s content already wraps acceptably.","Semantic line breaks matter: keeping “and any” together is better than a technically valid but awkward split."],"specific":["Free cannot go below 100px because “Community” is 79px plus 21px padding.","Pro cannot go below 87px because “Unlimited” is 66px plus 21px padding.","Notes needs about 246px to keep “Supports Okta, Azure AD and any” on one line; around 231px it becomes three lines with an orphan.","Enterprise’s “24/7 phone & dedicated manager” can wrap into two balanced lines at 170–180px without a third line."]},"tradeoffs":"A reasonable designer could prefer r3C’s 180px Enterprise and 246px Notes for a roomier plan column; the difference from r2C is only a few pixels and both preserve two-line rows. r3B’s 256px Notes produces a less balanced support-note break (“Response time targets are defined / in the SLA.”) but is still publishable.","uncertain":"The exact pixel threshold where Notes drops to three lines is font-metric sensitive; r2A at 243px is borderline and some designers would accept its break after “and.” Whether the 3-line row in r1C/r2B is a true fault or an acceptable tradeoff for a wider Enterprise column is also debatable."}
